drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: White's plan is Rb8+, checking along the back rank while his c5, d6 and e6 pawns keep rolling. Your Kd8 walked right into it: after Rb8+ your knight had to retreat to the passive c8 square, c6 pushed further, and White's other rook jumped into h7 — your small edge turned into a lost game. Kc8 avoids the whole problem; after c6 Bc4 dxe7 Kc7 Rb7+ you're still fighting because your king was never trapped on the back rank. In endgames with advanced connected passers, always check which king square keeps you off the rank a rook can invade.

drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: That d5 pawn was hanging, defended only by the e5 pawn, with your rook on a7 and knight on e7 both lined up to grab it. Instead you played Kd7, spending a move on king safety while the free pawn sat there; White answered Rxc5, snatching your c5 pawn instead, and after Rc8 e6+ your king got shoved around and the game swung from equal to clearly worse for you. Nxd5 wins the pawn outright — after Rxc5+ Rc7 Rbc6 Rxc6 Nxc6 you trade into an ending where you're simply a pawn up. Before playing a quiet improving move, scan for hanging pawns first; free material beats prophylaxis.
drills.threat: White's pawn on d5 is only guarded by the e5 pawn — your knight on e7 and rook both eye it.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king on g1 has nowhere to run — his own rook on h1 blocks one escape, the h3 pawn blocks another, and your rook already covers the second rank from f2. Instead of finishing with mate, you played Rxb2, grabbing a pawn, which let White breathe: Nd2 then Qc2 defends, Rh2 harasses your rook, and Qxd3 brings his queen back — still winning for you, but a forced mate shrank to just a big material edge. Qg2# ends it on the spot: your queen drops onto g2, backed by the rook on f2, and the king has no square left. Before cashing a free pawn, always check whether mate is already there.
drills.threat: White's king on g1 is boxed in by his own rook and pawn on h3 — one accurate move ends it.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's rooks on a1 and h1 are still at home and his king sits on h2 — give him one free move and he routes a rook to d1 or e1 to fight back. a6 didn't ask any questions; it just spent a tempo, so White answered Re1, traded down after Rde8, and calmly played b3 to stabilize — your near-five-pawn edge shrank to about three. Qf3 keeps the pressure on: your queen jumps into White's camp, and after Rd1 Rde8 Re1 Bd6 a4 you're still dictating play because White never got that free consolidating move. When you're up big, look for moves that keep asking questions instead of just shuffling.
drills.threat: White's rooks on a1 and h1 are still undeveloped — a free tempo lets him swing one to d1 or e1.

Qb3 fixes the real problem: it guards b2 and invites a trade, so after Rxb2 Qxb2 Nxb2 Kxb2 Kf8 you reach a plain endgame, worse but safe. drills.coachNote: With your king still uncastled on e1 and Black's bishop active on f5, the real danger isn't the c5 pawn — it's the bishop jumping into d3, right next to your king, the moment you look elsewhere. You played dxc5, picking off a pawn, and that let Black play Bd3 immediately; your knight had to retreat awkwardly to g1 just to survive, and you only castled several moves later than you should have. Kf1 fixes the priority — it tucks your king toward safety, and after a6 Qd1 Qb6 Nb3 Nc6 the game stays calm and balanced. When your king is stuck in the center, safety outranks grabbing a loose pawn.

drills.coachNote: Black's king is scrambling over to defend the e6/c7 pawns and dig in — in bishop endgames the exact square your king takes matters, since the wrong one lets his king hold things together. Kf4 looks natural, but it let Black play Kf7-Ke7 and consolidate, and what should've been a close-to-forced win got murky — your advantage dropped from nearly +20 to about +9, so the win got much harder than it needed to be. Kf3 keeps the king on the right side to support pushing e3-e4 and breaking through, and after Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 you march forward with tempo instead of giving Black time to settle. Take the extra second to check which square keeps your king shepherding the pawn break.

drills.title: vs Abfab18 (791) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Black's only real hope is racing the king to c8 or d8 to blockade your c6-pawn — that's the one drawing try left. Bb3 sits on the same a2-g8 diagonal, but it's the wrong square for this technique; the bishop had to backtrack to a2 anyway, and in those two lost tempi Black's king slipped to e7 and back to f7, shrinking a completely winning +19.8 down to a fraction of that. Ba2 skips the detour: Ke7, Kc4, Ke8, Kb5 and your king marches straight in to escort the pawn while the bishop still guards c8. In simple wins, put the piece on its final square the first time.

drills.coachNote: Black's rook on f2 defends d2 along the second rank, so if your king ever loses the f1 escape square, Qxd2 is mate. Rf1 walks right into that — it fills your own last flight square without touching the threat, so Qxd2# landed at once, turning a comfortable +5.6 into an instant loss. Qd7+ solves it by checking first: Kf6 is forced, and only then do you castle long with O-O-O, tucking your king to safety while keeping your full material edge. drills.coachNote: Black's rook on h5 has no defenders at all, and the king still sitting on e8 means a check could pick it off for free. Qd4 centralizes but creates no threat, so Black got a free move — Qd7 tucks the queen in to guard and reroute, and the loose rook escapes, dropping your edge from +6.2 to barely anything. Qg6+ is the move that actually exploits it: the check forces the king to move, and only then does Qxh5 grab the rook clean, with Nd4+ adding another check to keep the initiative rolling. drills.coachNote: White's a6 and b6 pawns are dangerously advanced and defended by the rook on e6 — your rook needs to get behind one of them, not chase the king. Rc4+ only kicks the king from e4 to d5, exactly the square it wants to reach to support the pawns' push, so it does nothing to slow them and next comes b7, shrinking your winning margin. Rc1 skips the wasted check and heads straight for b1, getting behind the pawn before it's urgent — after ...b7 you still have time for Re1+ first, then Rb1 parks in front of the pawn for good. In a pawn race, ask whether a check actually helps your king or your opponent's before you play it.

drills.coachNote: The a6 and b5 pawns are connected passers backed by the rook on e6, and if you don't blockade one of them right now, White just walks them down the board. Rc7 puts your rook on the wrong file — it doesn't touch either pawn, so White plays b6 then b7, and only then does your rook scramble c7-c1-a1 to finally get behind them, burning tempi you didn't have to spare. Ra7 gets behind the a6-pawn immediately, the one square that actually stops it cold, so White has to look for activity elsewhere with Re8, Kd6, Rg8+ while your structure holds. Against a passed pawn, get your rook behind it the moment you spot it — anywhere else is just decoration.
drills.threat: White's a6 and b5 pawns are connected and protected by the rook on e6 — they're closer to queening than they look.

drills.coachNote: Down a whole rook, Black's only practical try is activating the bishop and the d5/c4 pawns for any kind of resistance — every spare tempo helps that plan. Kc6 looks natural but lets Black in with Bg4, and by the time you've played Kd6, Kf8, Re7 the win has turned from a straight march into a murky grind, your edge sagging from +67.7 to barely a third of that. Kb4 keeps the king flexible, ready to swing to c5 and d6 without handing the bishop a free tempo — Bh3, Kc5, Kd8, Kd6 shepherds the black king straight into the corner. When you're completely winning, pick the square that keeps every option open before you march toward the action.

When your king is standing in a mating net, fix that before you do anything else on the board.

R3e4+ is a check, but it lets the king slide to g3, and then White grabs back with Kxh3 — swallowing your bishop — while you're left picking up only the d4 pawn with Rxd4. That's a huge chunk of your advantage given away for nothing, in a position that was already completely winning. g5 finishes the job immediately: it seals off the king's last flight squares and delivers mate on the spot, no further moves needed. When the enemy king is nearly boxed in, look for the move that closes the box rather than the move that merely checks it.

Bxg2 grabs a pawn but isn't check, so White gets that breather — Ra6 activates the rook, and after ...Bxh3 Kg3 the king escapes toward safety and even hits back with a check of his own on R8e3+, costing you a good slice of your winning advantage. g5+ keeps the king hunt alive instead: after g5+ Kf5 Rf2+ Kg4 Rxg2+ Kf5 you still pick up the g2 pawn, but with checks the whole way, so the king never gets to reorganize. When you've got a king on the run, keep it running — pausing to snack on a pawn can let it escape the net.

Ke3 heads straight for the real target instead — after Ke3 Kc2 a5 Kb1 Kxf3 Kc2 your king simply eats the f3 pawn and the rest collapses. When the opponent's only counterplay lives in one pawn cluster, march your king there instead of continuing your own pawn race.

drills.coachNote: White's whole survival plan is getting something going with that f3-g4-h5 pawn group, since he has nothing else left. Kd4 heads the wrong way, toward the queenside, so White gets to play f4 — after gxf4 Kc2 f3 you end up having to escort a pawn home the long way instead of simply vacuuming up White's structure, and a chunk of your winning margin evaporates in the process. Ke5 goes straight at the target: after Ke5 Kc2 Kf4 Kd3 a5 Ke2 your king marches right into White's pawns while his king is stuck babysitting the queenside, and the win becomes simple and fast. Even in a completely won endgame, send your king toward the opponent's only remaining chances, not away from them.

Rxe3 was the cleaner finish — it tears straight into the pawn shelter, and after Rh2, Ke2, cxd3+, Bxd3, White's king has no safe square left. Rh3# ended it on the spot instead: the king on h2 has no square left — g1 and g3 covered by your queen, g2 covered by your bishop on e4, h1 blocked by the rook itself. Principle: before giving a natural-looking check, make sure a key defender isn't quietly walking off its post — and always look for mate before anything else.

You jumped Nd2 immediately, and Rfd1 attacked it on the spot, forcing the knight straight back to e4 — two tempi spent to end up where you started, and White grabbed the initiative with c4 and dxc4 while you were busy retreating. The engine's idea was to play Rf6 first, repositioning the rook, and only after Rfe1 Re8 Rab1 does Nd2 actually work, this time landing safely and even winning material with Bxd5. Prepare the square a piece is jumping into before you commit it there — sequencing matters as much as the idea itself.
drills.threat: White's rooks on a1 and f1 can both swing onto the d-file in one move, and d2 isn't covered by anything of yours.

drills.coachNote: White's queen on g4 sits on the open diagonal g4-f5-e6-d7, and your knight on d7 is completely undefended. Kf8 ignored that, so White simply played Qxd7 — after Re6, Be3, Rae8 you were down a full piece for nothing, turning a fighting position into a lost one. Kh7 keeps you in it: it gets the king to safety, and after Bd2 Rg8 you stay active, with the forced Qe4+ Qg6 Qxg6+ only trading queens instead of costing material. Whenever a piece sits on the same diagonal as the enemy queen, that's the first thing to check before anything else.

drills.title: vs EddsSalinas (516) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: That knight on f7 already forks your queen on d8 and rook on h8 — you can't keep both. Nd5 ignored the fork entirely, so White played Qd6+, Ke8, Qxd8+, and Kxf7 handed him your queen for a knight, turning a position you were winning by almost five pawns into a roughly even one. Qg8 solves it: the queen steps off the fork while still covering h8, so after Nxh8 Qxh8 you only lose the exchange, not the queen, and stay clearly better. When two pieces are forked, save the more valuable one and count exactly what you're forced to give up.
drills.threat: White's knight on f7 forks your queen on d8 and your rook on h8 — both are hanging to it.

drills.title: vs EddsSalinas (516) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: The c3 pawn attacks your bishop on b4, so it has to move — but the knight on e4 also covers d6, the natural-looking retreat, and arrives there with check. Bd6 walked into exactly that: Nxd6+ forced Ke7, then the same knight jumped to f7, forking your queen on d8 and rook on h8 again, costing real material from a position you were winning by nearly four pawns. Bf8 sidesteps it — a quiet retreat that keeps the bishop safe, even though White still nets the e6 pawn later with Nxe6. Before retreating to a square, check whether the enemy already covers it.
drills.threat: Your bishop on b4 is attacked by the c3 pawn, and the knight on e4 covers d6 with check.

drills.coachNote: Your bishop on h6 sits on the h-file with black's queen on h4 staring right at it, undefended. Qxb7 grabbed a pawn but ignored that, so Black played Qxh6, winning the bishop and wiping out most of the huge lead you'd built. Bg7+ solves both problems at once — the bishop escapes while giving check, forcing Rxg7, and then Qxc8+ wins the exchange on the back rank: after Qd8 Qxd8+ Nxd8 you trade queens a full rook ahead. When one of your own pieces is hanging, look for the move that saves it and creates a threat, not just the biggest pawn available.

drills.coachNote: Both black's knight on e4 and queen on d8 bear on the g5 square, so it's not the safe outpost it looks like. Bg5 walked in anyway: Nxg5, Nxg5 looks like a clean trade, but then Qxg5 grabs your recapturing knight for free since nothing was left to guard it, dropping a full piece from a roughly balanced position. Bh2 keeps the bishop off that square entirely, tucked safely on the long diagonal, and lets you continue normal plans like Nc5 and Be2, pressing on black's central pawns instead. Before placing a piece on a square, check every attacker of it — including the ones that only show up after a trade goes through.

drills.title: vs Zaratustra25 (819) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Grabbing the pawn on c7 looks free, but black's rook on e8 immediately swings to c8 to challenge it. Rxc7 walked into that: after Rec8, Rxc8+, Rxc8, the rooks come off, and you're left in an ending where black's advanced pawns on b5 and e4 are simply faster than that extra pawn is worth. g4 ignores the free pawn and keeps your rook flexible instead — after Rac8, Rd5, Re6, Rc5, Ke8 your rook stays active on the fifth rank rather than getting traded away. When you're already worse in a rook ending, don't trade your active rook for a single pawn.
drills.threat: Black's rook on e8 is ready to meet Rxc7 with ...Rc8, trading rooks into a faster ending for him.
